title: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)
hookLine: a mother encourages her sons to hold fast to their faith under torture

cards: A mother and seven brothers are brought before the king. The second book of Maccabees, chapter seven, tells it plainly. The order is simple: eat the forbidden meat, and live.
One by one, the brothers refuse. The first to speak says: we are ready to die rather than break the laws of our fathers.
The text does not hide what follows; one after another, the sons are tortured and killed, each refusing, each speaking a few last words about God, some about a life beyond this one.
And one person in the room has to watch every moment. The chapter turns its eyes to her.

teach.b: The text calls her marvelous above all, worthy of honorable memory. She sees her sons die in a single day and bears it with good courage because of her hope in the Lord. And she doesn't stay silent.

teach.h: IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR FATHERS.
teach.b: She encourages each of them in the language of their fathers, with words about where life comes from: I don't know how you came to be in my womb. I didn't give you breath and life, or shape your body.
The Creator of the world did, and in mercy, he will give you breath and life again. Then the hardest scene. Only the youngest is left.
The king promises him riches and friendship if he'll turn, and asks the mother to talk him into it. She agrees to speak.

She leans toward her son and, in the family language, says: have pity on me, who carried you nine months and nursed you three years. Look at the heaven and the earth; God made them out of nothing. Don't be afraid.
Then the youngest refuses too. And last of all, the mother dies. The rabbis told their own version in the Talmud, tractate Gittin, set in a different time.

There, as the mother dies, a heavenly voice calls out a line from the Psalms, in the King James words: "a joyful mother of children." A strange, painful blessing. The story doesn't say she wasn't crushed.
It says that in that room, she encouraged them.

how: Jewish tradition remembers the mother and her seven sons as an example of kiddush ha-shem, sanctifying God's name, and some communities retell their story at Hanukkah and on Tisha b'Av.

games.q: you're the mother. six sons are gone. the king promises your youngest riches if he turns, and asks you to persuade him. what do you say?
o: save yourself; do what the king says.
nothing at all; you can't bear to speak.
have pity on me, look at heaven and earth, and don't be afraid.
games.why: she agrees to speak, then in the family language tells him not to fear. the king hoped she'd break him. she encouraged him.

practice: Bring to mind someone who raised you or stood beside you and was brave in a hard moment, a hospital, a border, a job lost, a quiet choice nobody else saw, and let them be as they were, not perfect, just brave once.
If no one comes, think of a parent in your community, or today's mother. If you pray, use words from your tradition to honor them.

wordCard.voice: Gittin, the Talmud tractate where the rabbis retold the mother and seven sons, ending with a joyful mother of children. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a joyful mother of children, from Psalm 113:9, the line the heavenly voice calls out in the Talmud's telling.

carryVoice: Your line: she encouraged them. She is remembered for her courage, not only her grief. See you tomorrow.
